questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cell membrane transport & body fluid compartments
questions.stem: Total body water in an average adult male constitutes approximately what percentage of body weight?
questions.concept: Of 60%, two-thirds is intracellular and one-third extracellular, of which a quarter is plasma. Women have lower total body water because of higher fat content, and infants higher at about 75%.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Body Fluids

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cell membrane transport & body fluid compartments
questions.stem: Plasma volume is measured using:
options: Evans blue dye or radioiodinated albumin
questions.concept: The indicator dilution principle requires a marker confined to the compartment measured: inulin or mannitol for extracellular fluid, deuterium or tritiated water for total body water, and albumin-bound markers for plasma.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Body Fluids

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cell membrane transport & body fluid compartments
questions.stem: The sodium-potassium ATPase pump moves:
options: Three sodium out for every two potassium in, making it electrogenic
Two sodium out, three potassium in
questions.concept: This unequal exchange contributes directly to the resting membrane potential and consumes a large share of basal metabolic energy. Digoxin inhibits it, raising intracellular sodium and calcium.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Cell Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cell membrane transport & body fluid compartments
questions.stem: Facilitated diffusion differs from active transport in that it:
options: Requires no energy and moves solute down its concentration gradient
questions.concept: Both are carrier-mediated and show saturation and competition, but facilitated diffusion cannot move solute against a gradient. Glucose entry via GLUT transporters is the classic example.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Cell Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cell membrane transport & body fluid compartments
questions.stem: The principal determinant of plasma oncotic pressure is:
questions.concept: Albumin contributes about 75 to 80% of oncotic pressure because of its abundance and small size. Hypoalbuminaemia in nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis and malnutrition therefore causes generalised oedema.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Body Fluids

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cell membrane transport & body fluid compartments
questions.stem: Starling forces determining fluid movement across a capillary include all EXCEPT:
questions.concept: Net filtration depends on the balance of hydrostatic and oncotic pressures across the capillary wall, modified by the reflection coefficient. Sodium determines osmolality but not transcapillary fluid balance directly.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Circulation

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cell membrane transport & body fluid compartments
questions.stem: Plasma osmolality is calculated approximately as:
options: Twice the sodium plus glucose/18 plus urea/2.8 in conventional units
questions.concept: Normal osmolality is 285 to 295 mOsm/kg. A raised osmolar gap between measured and calculated values suggests unmeasured osmoles such as methanol, ethylene glycol or mannitol.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Body Fluids

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cell membrane transport & body fluid compartments
questions.stem: The Donnan effect describes:
options: Unequal distribution of diffusible ions due to non-diffusible charged proteins on one side
questions.concept: Impermeant plasma proteins carry negative charge, attracting slightly more cations into plasma, which contributes to the effective oncotic pressure beyond that predicted by protein concentration alone.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Body Fluids

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cell membrane transport & body fluid compartments
questions.stem: Aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct are regulated by:
options: Antidiuretic hormone acting through V2 receptors and cyclic AMP
questions.concept: ADH causes insertion of preformed aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane, permitting water reabsorption. Absence causes central diabetes insipidus, and receptor or channel defects cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Renal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cell membrane transport & body fluid compartments
questions.stem: Infusion of isotonic saline expands:
options: The extracellular compartment only, with no change in cell volume
questions.concept: Isotonic fluid creates no osmotic gradient, so it stays extracellular. Five percent dextrose is effectively free water after glucose metabolism and distributes through all compartments, making it a poor resuscitation fluid.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Body Fluids

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Muscle physiology: skeletal, smooth & cardiac contraction
questions.stem: In skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling, calcium binds to:
options: Troponin C, moving tropomyosin to expose actin binding sites
questions.concept: In smooth muscle, by contrast, calcium binds calmodulin activating myosin light chain kinase - the fundamental difference between the two mechanisms and the basis of different drug actions.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Muscle Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Muscle physiology: skeletal, smooth & cardiac contraction
questions.stem: During muscle contraction, which band remains constant in length?
questions.concept: The A band represents thick filament length which does not change; the I band and H zone shorten as thin filaments slide inward. This is the essence of the sliding filament theory.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Muscle Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Muscle physiology: skeletal, smooth & cardiac contraction
questions.stem: Rigor mortis occurs because:
options: ATP depletion prevents detachment of myosin heads from actin
questions.concept: ATP is required not for the power stroke but for cross-bridge release, so its depletion after death locks the muscles. Rigor appears in 1 to 2 hours, is complete by 12 hours and passes off with putrefaction.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Muscle Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Muscle physiology: skeletal, smooth & cardiac contraction
questions.stem: Cardiac muscle differs from skeletal muscle in that it:
options: Has a long plateau phase preventing tetanic contraction
questions.concept: The prolonged calcium-mediated plateau gives a refractory period lasting nearly the whole contraction, so cardiac muscle cannot summate or tetanise - an essential protection allowing the heart to fill.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Cardiac Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Muscle physiology: skeletal, smooth & cardiac contraction
questions.stem: The functional syncytium of cardiac muscle depends on:
options: Gap junctions in the intercalated discs
questions.concept: Gap junctions permit rapid ion flow so the atria and ventricles each contract as a unit, while the fibrous skeleton insulates them electrically, with the AV node as the sole normal conduction pathway.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Cardiac Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Muscle physiology: skeletal, smooth & cardiac contraction
questions.stem: Smooth muscle differs from skeletal muscle in that it:
options: Can maintain tension with low energy expenditure through the latch mechanism
questions.concept: The latch state allows sustained tone in vessels, gut and airways at minimal metabolic cost. Smooth muscle also lacks troponin and has no striations, using the calmodulin pathway instead.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Muscle Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Muscle physiology: skeletal, smooth & cardiac contraction
questions.stem: The neuromuscular junction transmitter and receptor are:
questions.concept: Myasthenia gravis results from antibodies to these postsynaptic nicotinic receptors, giving fatigable weakness that improves with anticholinesterases - the basis of both the disease and its treatment.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Synaptic Transmission

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Muscle physiology: skeletal, smooth & cardiac contraction
questions.stem: The Frank-Starling law of the heart states that:
options: Force of contraction increases with increased initial fibre length up to a point
questions.concept: Increased venous return stretches sarcomeres to optimal overlap and increases troponin C calcium sensitivity, so the heart pumps whatever it receives - the mechanism matching right and left ventricular outputs.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Cardiac Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Muscle physiology: skeletal, smooth & cardiac contraction
questions.stem: Isometric contraction is characterised by:
options: Increased tension without change in muscle length
questions.concept: Isotonic contraction shortens at constant load. Cardiac isovolumetric contraction is the isometric phase between mitral closure and aortic opening, when pressure rises without ejection.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Muscle Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Muscle physiology: skeletal, smooth & cardiac contraction
questions.stem: Muscle fatigue during sustained exercise is primarily due to:
options: Accumulation of metabolites and impaired excitation-contraction coupling rather than ATP depletion
questions.concept: ATP rarely falls below about 60% of resting levels. Accumulation of inorganic phosphate and hydrogen ions and impaired sarcoplasmic calcium release are the dominant mechanisms in peripheral fatigue.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Muscle Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Blood: haemopoiesis, haemostasis, blood groups
questions.stem: The main site of haemopoiesis in an adult is:
options: The red marrow of flat bones and proximal ends of long bones
questions.concept: In fetal life the yolk sac, then liver and spleen are the sites; after birth the marrow takes over, retracting to the axial skeleton by adulthood. Extramedullary haemopoiesis resumes in marrow failure or myelofibrosis.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Blood

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Blood: haemopoiesis, haemostasis, blood groups
questions.stem: Erythropoietin is produced mainly by:
options: Peritubular interstitial cells of the kidney in response to hypoxia
questions.concept: This explains the normocytic anaemia of chronic kidney disease and the response to recombinant erythropoietin. Around 10% comes from the liver, which cannot compensate for renal loss.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Blood

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Blood: haemopoiesis, haemostasis, blood groups
questions.stem: The intrinsic pathway of coagulation is assessed by:
questions.concept: APTT assesses the intrinsic and common pathways and monitors heparin; PT with INR assesses the extrinsic pathway and monitors warfarin. Factor VII of the extrinsic pathway has the shortest half-life.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Blood

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Blood: haemopoiesis, haemostasis, blood groups
questions.stem: Vitamin K dependent clotting factors are:
options: II, VII, IX and X with proteins C and S
questions.concept: Gamma-carboxylation confers calcium-binding capacity. Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, and the early fall in protein C explains transient hypercoagulability at initiation.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Blood

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Blood: haemopoiesis, haemostasis, blood groups
questions.stem: Primary haemostasis refers to:
options: Formation of the platelet plug through adhesion, activation and aggregation
questions.concept: Von Willebrand factor bridges platelet GpIb to collagen, and fibrinogen bridges GpIIb/IIIa between platelets. Defects here prolong bleeding time and cause mucocutaneous bleeding, unlike coagulation defects which cause deep bleeding.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Blood

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Blood: haemopoiesis, haemostasis, blood groups
questions.stem: An individual with blood group O has:
options: Anti-A and anti-B antibodies in plasma with no A or B antigens on red cells
questions.concept: Group O red cells are the universal donor while AB plasma is the universal donor for plasma - the relationship is inverted between components, a frequent examination point.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Blood

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Blood: haemopoiesis, haemostasis, blood groups
questions.stem: Haemolytic disease of the newborn from Rh incompatibility typically affects:
options: The second and subsequent Rh-positive pregnancies of an Rh-negative mother
questions.concept: Sensitisation usually occurs at delivery of the first Rh-positive infant, so the first pregnancy is spared. Anti-D immunoglobulin given antenatally and within 72 hours of delivery prevents sensitisation.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Blood

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Blood: haemopoiesis, haemostasis, blood groups
questions.stem: Plasmin is generated from plasminogen by:
questions.concept: Plasmin degrades fibrin producing D-dimers, which is why D-dimer is raised in venous thromboembolism and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Tranexamic acid blocks plasminogen binding to fibrin.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Blood

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Blood: haemopoiesis, haemostasis, blood groups
questions.stem: The lifespan of a normal red blood cell is about:
questions.concept: Platelets survive 7 to 10 days and neutrophils only hours in the circulation. The 120-day red cell lifespan underlies the use of HbA1c as a 3-month glycaemic index, which is unreliable in haemolysis.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Blood

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Blood: haemopoiesis, haemostasis, blood groups
questions.stem: Thrombin has which of the following actions?
options: Converts fibrinogen to fibrin, activates factors V, VIII, XI and XIII and activates platelets
questions.concept: Thrombin is the central amplifying enzyme of coagulation, and also activates protein C via thrombomodulin, providing negative feedback that localises the clot to the site of injury.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Blood
